name: Rhaponticum carthamoides (maral root)

lead: Maral root is a Siberian alpine herb whose roots contain large amounts of 20-hydroxyecdysone, an ecdysteroid that acts as a molting hormone in insects. Lifters take it hoping for faster recovery, better protein synthesis and more muscle mass, and it is also used as an adaptogen.

The muscle claim rests on its ecdysteroid content. Published literature on the plant is mostly chemistry and laboratory work, including antioxidant and other activities, and the sources reviewed contain no human trial of it for muscle or appearance.

paras: It is taken as an extract or powder in capsules, usually alongside resistance training and often stacked with other muscle or adaptogen supplements. Users generally run it for several weeks while judging gym recovery and progress.
Human safety data are not covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a supplement, and products can be confused with Rheum rhaponticum, a different plant, so the label species matters.

angle.text: Maral root is sold to lifters as an ecdysteroid-rich herb: the ecdysteroids are claimed to support protein synthesis and recovery, leading to more muscle. The muscle claims rest on animal data and user reports.

lead: Rhaponticum carthamoides (synonym Leuzea carthamoides), known as maral root or Russian leuzea, is a perennial herb of the daisy family (Asteraceae) that grows wild in southern Siberia, Kazakhstan, the Altai and the western Sayan Mountains at sub-alpine and alpine elevations.[1] Its roots are rich in 20-hydroxyecdysone (ecdysterone), an ecdysteroid that acts as a molting hormone in arthropods.[1][2]

In muscle-building circles it is sold as an adaptogen and as a plant source of ecdysteroids. The appearance case made by supplement users is a chain: ecdysteroids are said to support protein synthesis and training capacity, which in turn would allow more training and more muscle, and adaptogen claims add better recovery. Traditional use in eastern Russia, where it has been used for centuries as a tonic, is the basis for the adaptogen label.[2]

Published literature on the whole plant is mostly phytochemical and pharmacological reviews with in vitro and animal work. Human trials exist for isolated ecdysterone and for an ecdysterone-based drug in giardiasis, but no completed human trial of maral root itself for muscle or appearance outcomes was found.[2][3][4]

paras: The common name maral root (maralu) is said to come from the maral deer, which reportedly feed on the plant, though Wikipedia flags that etymology as needing a source.[1] Eight synonyms are listed there, including Leuzea carthamoides, Cnicus carthamoides, Cirsium carthamoides and Stemmacantha carthamoides.[1] The plant grows wild at roughly 1,400 to 1,800 metres in sub-alpine zones and in alpine meadows, and is described as grown in cultivation in Russia and Eastern Europe.[1] A 1985 USSR postage stamp showing it appeared in a series on medicinal plants of Siberia.[1]
The name is easily confused with Rheum rhaponticum, rhubarb, whose extract ERr 731 has been tested in menopausal women; it is a different plant.[5]

A 2009 review in Phytochemistry, drawing on 117 sources, many in Russian, describes maral root as having been used for centuries in eastern Russia for its medicinal properties.[2] Maral root is described in the literature as a traditional Siberian folk-medicine plant used as a stimulant to boost overall health and fitness.[6] Plant adaptogen research began in the 1960s, and a 2021 review reports that plant adaptogens including Rhaponticum carthamoides were first used in professional sports about 50 years earlier, owing to their reputed ability to increase resistance to stress and physical endurance.[7] The plant is among those covered in the Russian Pharmacopoeia reviews.[8]

The Phytochemistry review catalogued more than 120 structures from the plant. The main groups are steroids, especially ecdysteroids, and phenolics (flavonoids and phenolic acids), accompanied by polyacetylenes, sesquiterpene lactones, triterpenoid glycosides and essential oil terpenes. Reported pharmacological effects of its extracts and compounds include actions on the brain, blood, cardiovascular and nervous systems and on proteosynthesis, work capacity, reproduction and sexual function, based largely on animal and laboratory work.[2] Chemical analysis of ecdysteroids in maral root is described as difficult because many related structures have similar chromatographic behaviour.[6]

20-hydroxyecdysone, the plant's headline ecdysteroid, acts through the ecdysone receptor in arthropods. Mammals lack that receptor; Wikipedia's article on the compound says it is hypothesised to act on estrogen receptor beta, which is linked to muscle hypertrophy, and that oral bioavailability is described as high.[9] Other studies have reported antimicrobial activity of crude extracts from Siberian medicinal plants including this species, and identified radical-scavenging compounds in it.[10][11] A 2023 paper in Nutrients examined anti-adipogenic activity of the plant and its secondary metabolites in cell work.[12]
Reviews of adaptogens list Rhaponticum carthamoides alongside ginseng, Eleutherococcus, Rhodiola and Schisandra and describe stress-protective mechanisms mostly in cell and animal models.[7][13]

Ecdysterone and the related turkesterone occur in Rhaponticum carthamoides, spinach, quinoa and Ajuga turkestanica, and a 2024 review in Nutrients discusses their possible advantages for general health and athletic performance as well as proposed uses in fatigue and cardiovascular and neurodegenerative conditions.[3]

Wikipedia's article on 20-hydroxyecdysone describes a 2019 Archives of Toxicology study by Isenmann and colleagues, funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency, in which participants dosed with ecdysterone showed significantly greater gains in muscle mass and bench press strength; the article does not give the sample size or design. It also cites a 2006 study by Wilborn and colleagues in which 30 mg a day orally did not significantly affect body composition or training adaptations in resistance-trained men, and earlier mostly Russian-language reports from 1986 to 1998 that claimed anabolic effects.[9] These studies concern the isolated compound, not maral root extract, whose ecdysteroid content varies by product.

The Phytochemistry review includes a discussion of the plant's toxicity.[2] A laboratory paper reported that a transformed-root extract reduced the viability of human glioma cells in culture, a cell finding without clinical meaning for supplement users.[14] Wikipedia describes 20-hydroxyecdysone as appearing to have little or no effect on non-transgenic animals at usual doses while not being totally inert, and lists its pregnancy category as unknown.[9]

Maral root is sold as a dietary supplement, typically as root powder or extract, sometimes in blends with other ecdysteroid sources. In the US the isolated compound is listed as over-the-counter and described as not generally regulated.[9] Supplement sellers market it for strength and recovery, usually by reference to its 20-hydroxyecdysone content; the research cited above does not include a trial of the marketed products.

No studies found for maral root in muscle growth, recovery or appearance. Human trials exist for ecdysten, a drug based on ecdysterone isolated from Rhaponticum carthamoides, in giardiasis: a 10-day course produced clinical and parasitological recovery in 22 of 32 patients with persistent giardiasis (68.7 percent) in a 2002 report, and a later controlled trial compared it with metronidazole.[4][15] Other related research is limited to laboratory and animal work on the plant and its constituents, and to trials of a different plant, Rheum rhaponticum (rhubarb extract ERr 731), which has a confusingly similar name and was tested in menopausal women.[5]

lore.intro: Maral root is mentioned in supplement and muscle-building contexts as a plant ecdysteroid source and adaptogen.[2][7]
